You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/locale/nl.js. Once it is fixed, a test named `Format Day of Month Do 1 - 31` should pass (the exact test is NOT in the repository; its name describes the expected behaviour: formatting the day of month with the `Do` token must produce the correct Dutch ordinal for every day 1..31, e.g. 1 -> '1e', 2 -> '2e', ... and any exceptions Dutch uses).

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/locale/nl.js and compare it with other locales in /dayjs/src/locale/ that implement `ordinal` (e.g. en.js, de.js, fr.js, and especially any locale with a similar ordinal rule). Understand how the core calls `ordinal` (see /dayjs/src/index.js format/`Do` handling) and what the locale's `formats`, `months`, `weekdays` etc. should be.
2. Determine the correct Dutch ordinal rule (Dutch ordinals are formed by adding 'e' to the number, with no irregular forms; verify against how other locales do it and against the locale's own documentation/comments in the file). Fix the bug with a MINIMAL edit to src/locale/nl.js. Do NOT modify any test file.
3. Verify: write a scratch script outside the repo (e.g. /tmp/nl_check.js) that imports dayjs and the nl locale (via `cd /dayjs && npx babel-node /tmp/nl_check.js` — check how other tests import locales, e.g. test/locale/*.test.js, and use the same import style) and prints `dayjs('2018-01-01').locale('nl').format('Do')` for days 1..31, checking each is '<n>e'. Also verify the rest of the locale still formats correctly (e.g. format('MMMM D, YYYY'), weekday names). Delete the scratch file afterwards.
4. Run the locale tests: `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/locale/nl.test.js --coverage=false` if it exists, plus `cd /dayjs && npx jest --coverage=false` for the full suite. Record which tests fail before your change and after.

Report back: the exact bug, the exact diff (file + lines), the commands run, and their before/after results.

You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/plugin/weekYear/index.js. Once it is fixed, a test named `yearStart: 4` should pass (the exact test is NOT in the repository; its name describes the expected behaviour: the weekYear plugin's `yearStart` option must be honored, i.e. a week-year configuration where the first week of the year is the week containing January 4th — the ISO-8601 rule — must produce the correct week-year for dates near year boundaries, e.g. 2018-12-31 is week-year 2019, 2019-01-01 is week-year 2019, 2017-01-01 is week-year 2016, etc. Note: ISO week numbering is the week containing the first Thursday / equivalently January 4th).

IMPORTANT: other subagents are concurrently fixing bugs in OTHER files (src/plugin/timezone/index.js, src/locale/nl.js). Do NOT touch those files. Only edit src/plugin/weekYear/index.js (and, only if strictly necessary and clearly part of the same bug, its closely related plugin files such as src/plugin/weekOfYear/index.js — but prefer to keep changes in weekYear). Never modify any test file.

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/plugin/weekYear/index.js, /dayjs/src/plugin/weekOfYear/index.js, /dayjs/src/plugin/isoWeek/index.js (if present), and the core /dayjs/src/index.js to understand how weekYear/weekOfYear are computed and how the `yearStart` option is supposed to be used (search the repo for `yearStart` — docs/, README, types/, tests).
2. Determine the correct behavior from in-repo sources (docstrings, docs, types, existing tests) and fix the bug with a MINIMAL edit. Do NOT modify any test file.
3. Verify: write a scratch script outside the repo (e.g. /tmp/wy_check.js) and run it with `cd /dayjs && npx babel-node /tmp/wy_check.js` (mirror the import style of test/plugin/weekYear.test.js). Check weekYear() and week()/weekOfYear() for dates: 2018-12-30, 2018-12-31, 2019-01-01, 2019-01-06, 2019-01-07, 2017-01-01, 2016-01-01, 2015-12-31, 2020-12-31, 2021-01-01, and compare with moment's isoWeekYear/isoWeek (`moment(...).isoWeekYear()`, `.isoWeek()`). Also test the yearStart option (e.g. `dayjs.extend(weekYear)` then `dayjs.Ls.en.weekStart`/`yearStart` or however the plugin reads it — read the code and docs to see how yearStart is configured) with yearStart: 4 and confirm results match ISO. Delete the scratch file afterwards.
4. Run: `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/plugin/weekYear.test.js --coverage=false` and the full suite `cd /dayjs && npx jest --coverage=false`. Record which tests fail BEFORE your change (run it first) and AFTER.

Report back: the exact bug and root cause, the exact diff (file + lines), the commands run, and their before/after results.

You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/plugin/timezone/index.js. Once it is fixed, a test named `Parse parse timestamp, js Date, Day.js object` (in test/plugin/timezone.test.js style, the exact version checking this behaviour may not exist in the repo) should pass — the test name describes the expected behaviour: parsing a timestamp, a native JS Date, and a Day.js object with the timezone plugin should produce correct results (e.g. dayjs.tz(timestamp, 'America/New_York'), dayjs.tz(new Date(...), tz), dayjs.tz(dayjsObject, tz), and .tz(tz) on an existing dayjs instance should all convert correctly, and the resulting value's internal $d / valueOf should be the correct UTC instant while the displayed time is in the target zone).

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/plugin/timezone/index.js carefully and find the real bug(s) in how inputs are parsed/converted (compare with how the plugin is documented in the file's docstring/README and how the rest of the repo behaves).
2. Fix the bug by editing the source file in place. Do NOT modify any existing test files.
3. Verify: run the existing test suite for the timezone plugin (e.g. `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/plugin/timezone.test.js` or `npm test -- test/plugin/timezone.test.js`; check package.json for the right command). Also write a temporary scratch script (outside the repo test dir, e.g. /tmp/check.js) that exercises: dayjs.tz(1234567891011, 'America/New_York'), dayjs.tz(new Date(1234567891011), 'America/New_York'), dayjs.tz(dayjs(1234567891011), 'America/New_York'), dayjs(1234567891011).tz('America/New_York') and confirm they all give the same correct instant and correct formatted local time. Delete the scratch script afterwards.
4. Make sure no pre-existing passing tests break: run the full test suite `cd /dayjs && npx jest` (or npm test) before and after your change and report which tests fail before and after.

Report back: the exact bug, the exact diff you made (file + lines), the test commands you ran, and their results (before/after).

You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js. Once it is fixed, two tests named `meridiem locale AM` and `meridiem locale PM` should pass (the exact tests are NOT in the repository; their names describe the expected behaviour: when parsing with the customParseFormat plugin using a format containing the `A`/`a` meridiem token, the locale's own meridiem strings (e.g. `dayjs.Ls[locale].meridiem` / the `meridiem` function of the locale, as used by the format plugin) must be honored — so a locale whose AM/PM strings differ from the English ones (e.g. zh-cn: 上午/下午, or a locale defining meridiem as a function) must parse correctly, and English 'AM'/'PM' must still parse).

IMPORTANT: other subagents are concurrently fixing bugs in OTHER files (src/plugin/timezone/index.js, src/locale/nl.js, src/plugin/weekYear/index.js). Do NOT touch those files. Only edit src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js. Never modify any test file.

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js and /dayjs/src/plugin/advancedFormat/index.js, plus /dayjs/src/index.js (format/parse internals) and a few locales that define `meridiem` (search the repo for `meridiem` in src/locale and src/plugin). Understand how the plugin handles the `A`/`a` tokens and where it fails to consult the locale.
2. Fix the bug with a MINIMAL edit to src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js. Do NOT modify any test file.
3. Verify: write a scratch script outside the repo (e.g. /tmp/cpf_check.js) run with `cd /dayjs && npx babel-node /tmp/cpf_check.js` (mirror the import style of test/plugin/customParseFormat.test.js). Test parsing with locales: default en ('h:mm A' with '5:00 PM' and '5:00 AM'), and at least one non-English locale that defines meridiem strings (find one in src/locale, e.g. zh-cn) — parse its local AM/PM strings and confirm the resulting hour is correct (13:00 for PM, 01:00 for AM). Also confirm existing behaviour (e.g. parsing '2018-01-01' etc.) is unchanged. Delete the scratch file afterwards.
4. Run: `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/plugin/customParseFormat.test.js --coverage=false` and the full suite `cd /dayjs && npx jest --coverage=false`. Record which tests fail BEFORE your change (run it first) and AFTER.

Report back: the exact bug and root cause, the exact diff (file + lines), the commands run, and their before/after results.

You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/plugin/duration/index.js. Once it is fixed, a test named `Creating milliseconds` should pass (the exact test is NOT in the repository; its name describes the expected behaviour: `dayjs.duration(...)` must support creating a duration from a number of milliseconds, e.g. `dayjs.duration(1000).asSeconds() === 1`, `dayjs.duration(1500).milliseconds() === 500`, `dayjs.duration(1000 * 60 * 60 * 24).asDays() === 1`, `dayjs.duration(500).asMilliseconds() === 500`, and `dayjs.duration(1000).as('milliseconds') === 1000`).

IMPORTANT: other subagents are concurrently fixing bugs in OTHER files (src/plugin/timezone/index.js, src/locale/nl.js, src/plugin/weekYear/index.js, src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js). Do NOT touch those files. Only edit src/plugin/duration/index.js. Never modify any test file.

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/plugin/duration/index.js completely, plus /dayjs/test/plugin/duration.test.js (read-only) and the duration docs in /dayjs/docs if present, and /dayjs/types/plugin/duration.d.ts. Understand how a duration is constructed from a number (should be milliseconds), from an object, from an ISO 8601 string, and how `asMilliseconds`/`asSeconds`/`as`/`milliseconds()`/`valueOf()` work.
2. Find the real bug in the millisecond construction path and fix it with a MINIMAL edit. Do NOT modify any test file.
3. Verify: write a scratch script outside the repo (e.g. /tmp/dur_check.js) run with `cd /dayjs && npx babel-node /tmp/dur_check.js` (mirror the import style of test/plugin/duration.test.js). Check: dayjs.duration(1000).asMilliseconds() === 1000, .asSeconds() === 1, .asMinutes() === 1/60, dayjs.duration(1500).milliseconds() === 500, dayjs.duration(1000*60*60*24).asDays() === 1, dayjs.duration(0).asMilliseconds() === 0, dayjs.duration(-1000).asMilliseconds() === -1000, and compare with moment.duration(...) equivalents. Also confirm object/ISO-string construction and existing behaviours still work. Delete the scratch file afterwards.
4. Run: `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/plugin/duration.test.js --coverage=false` and the full suite `cd /dayjs && npx jest --coverage=false`. Record which tests fail BEFORE your change (run it first) and AFTER.

Report back: the exact bug and root cause, the exact diff (file + lines), the commands run, and their before/after results.

You are working in the git repository checked out at /dayjs (the dayjs JavaScript date library). There is a bug in /dayjs/src/plugin/timezone/index.js. Once it is fixed, a test named `Convert format Z` should pass (the exact version of that test is NOT in the repository; its name describes the expected behaviour: after converting a date into a timezone with the timezone plugin, formatting with the `Z` token must show the correct UTC offset of that timezone, e.g. dayjs('2014-06-01T12:00:00Z').tz('America/Los_Angeles').format('Z') === '-07:00', and similarly for other zones/DST dates; also dayjs.tz('2014-06-01 12:00', 'America/New_York').format('Z') === '-04:00').

IMPORTANT: another subagent is concurrently fixing a DIFFERENT bug in the SAME file (src/plugin/timezone/index.js) — the input parsing of dayjs.tz() for timestamps / native Date / Day.js objects. So:
- Re-read the file immediately before every edit (it may have changed).
- Make MINIMAL, targeted edits only in the code path responsible for your bug; do not rewrite unrelated functions or reformat the file.
- Never revert or undo lines you did not write; if you see changes you did not make, keep them.
- Do not modify any test file.

Your job:
1. Read /dayjs/src/plugin/timezone/index.js and the core formatter in /dayjs/src/index.js (and /dayjs/src/constant.js) to understand how the `Z` token and utcOffset are computed, and why the offset is wrong after a timezone conversion (look at proto.tz: it uses `toLocaleString` and `new Date(target)` and `utcOffset(localUtcOffset - diff, true)`; consider fractional diffs, DST, and the `$offset`/`$u` handling).
2. Fix the bug with a minimal edit to the source (no test edits).
3. Verify with a scratch script outside the repo (e.g. /tmp/check2.js run via `cd /dayjs && npx babel-node /tmp/check2.js` or by writing a temporary jest test in /tmp — do NOT add files under /dayjs/test): check format('Z') for dayjs('2014-06-01T12:00:00Z').tz('America/Los_Angeles'), .tz('America/New_York'), .tz('Asia/Tokyo'), .tz('Europe/London'), a December (DST-off) date, and dayjs.tz('2014-06-01 12:00', 'America/New_York').format('Z'); compare each against moment-timezone's equivalent. Also check .format() and .valueOf() and .utcOffset() still match moment-timezone. Delete the scratch file afterwards.
4. Run the timezone test suite: `cd /dayjs && npx jest test/plugin/timezone.test.js --coverage=false` and also the full suite `cd /dayjs && npx jest --coverage=false` (note: some tests may already fail before your change — record the baseline first with `git stash`-free means, i.e. just run it before editing). Report which tests failed before and after your change.

Report back: the exact bug and root cause, the exact diff (file + lines), the commands run, and their before/after results.
